title: 3-SAT: brute force vs Schöning's random walk
problem_statement: Given a CNF formula over Boolean variables x_1..x_n in which every clause has at most 3 literals, decide whether some assignment satisfies every clause.

input.parameter: n = number of variables; m denotes the number of clauses (O-bounds read m as max(m, 1)).
input.size_measure: m clauses of at most 3 literals each: O(m log n) bits. The harness uses at most 6n + 8 clauses (m = Theta(n) for n >= 3).

algorithms.name: brute force
algorithms.idea: Enumerate all 2^n assignments and evaluate the formula on each, abandoning an assignment at its first falsified clause.
algorithms.pseudocode: for each assignment a in {0,1}^n: if every clause has a true literal under a: return True; return False
algorithms.time_complexity: O(2^n m) worst case (2^n assignments, O(m) clause checks each); all 2^n assignments are examined on every unsatisfiable formula
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive: every assignment is tried once, and True is returned exactly when one satisfies every clause (PROOFS.md section 1).

algorithms.name: Schöning's random walk (Monte Carlo, one-sided error)
algorithms.idea: Repeat T(n) times: start from a uniformly random assignment, and 3n times pick the first falsified clause and flip a uniformly random one of its variables. Answer True as soon as an assignment satisfies the formula; False after all tries.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(T(n) n m) with T(n) = ceil(ln(10^6) / p(n)) = Theta((4/3)^n sqrt(n)) tries: O((4/3)^n n^1.5 m) on every input; on unsatisfiable formulas without an empty clause every try runs to the end, i.e. all T(n)(3n + 1) clause scans, each stopping at the first falsified clause (between 1 and m clause checks); p(n) is the per-try success lower bound in caveats (PROOFS.md sections 3 and 4)
algorithms.correctness: Algorithm: Schöning 1999; proofs: PROOFS.md section 2. A True answer is always correct (a satisfying assignment was found). For a satisfiable formula fix a solution a*. Every flip of a variable in the first falsified clause decreases the distance to a* with probability >= 1/3. Coupling the flips with independent Bernoulli(1/3) steps shows that a try starting at distance j succeeds with probability >= C(3j,j) (1/3)^(2j) (2/3)^j, so one try succeeds with probability >= p(n) = sum_j C(n,j) 2^-n C(3j,j) (1/3)^(2j) (2/3)^j, and T(n) independent tries miss with probability <= exp(-p(n) T(n)) <= 10^-6.

relationship: O(2^n m) -> O((4/3)^n poly(n)) for a Monte Carlo algorithm with one-sided error 10^-6: a smaller exponential base, still exponential (secondary T8). The primary tag T6 rests on the NP-completeness of 3-SAT, which is background (cited, not proved here).

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle (a DPLL solver with unit propagation, in harness.py) on random 3-CNF (m = 2n, 4.26n, 6n), planted satisfiable 3-CNF (m = 5n), unsatisfiable formulas (random clauses plus all 8 sign patterns on one variable triple), mixed 1-/2-/3-literal formulas and the n = 0, 1, 2 edge cases, n = 0..12 (both algorithms) and n = 14 (Schöning and the oracle only), 6 instances per n. Schöning's answers are random but reproducible (the validator re-seeds `random` before each call). Not raised to V2, for two measured reasons. (1) On the unsatisfiable timing family (random 3-CNF with m = 5n plus 8 forcing clauses), experiments/2026-10-07_3sat_timing_probe.py measured Schöning at n = 4..12 with alpha = 0.960 against (4/3)^n n^2.5, but also 1.225 against (4/3)^n n^1.5 and 0.865 against 2^n. Over the n range that pure Python can time, the fit therefore cannot tell the claimed bound from brute force's 2^n. On unsatisfiable inputs the running time is in any case fixed by the restart budget T(n), by construction. (2) On planted formulas with a unique solution (n = 6..16, 5 instances x 4000 tries each), experiments/2026-10-07_schoening_planted_success.py measured per-try success rates 5.7 to 15 times above p(n) (empirical base about 0.82 per variable, against 0.71 for p(n) over the same range), so that family does not attain the bound. Brute force alone does fit its 2^n factor on the unsatisfiable family (alpha = 1.016 against 2^n over n = 8..16; it makes 6.6 to 8.2 clause checks per assignment there for n = 4..14, 0.24 m at n = 4 and 0.10 m at n = 14 (measured)).

caveats: Schöning's algorithm is randomized with one-sided error. With T(n) = ceil(ln(10^6) / p(n)) tries a satisfiable formula is wrongly reported unsatisfiable with probability at most 10^-6 per call; unsatisfiable formulas are always answered correctly. Hence the V1 agreement on satisfiable instances is itself probabilistic, although reproducible under the validator's seeding. The V1 battery contains 53 satisfiable and 31 unsatisfiable formulas (counted with the oracle). With fresh randomness, the probability that Schöning misses any of the satisfiable ones is at most 53 x 10^-6 (union bound). Here p(n) = sum_{j=0..n} C(n,j) 2^-n C(3j,j) (1/3)^(2j) (2/3)^j is an explicit lower bound on one try's success probability (PROOFS.md section 2.4: a coupling of the walk with independent Bernoulli(1/3) steps toward a fixed solution). For n = 14..20 it lies between 0.87 and 0.89 times (3/4)^n / sqrt(n) (computed). For every n >= 0, 0.431 (3/4)^n sqrt(3/(n + 3)) <= p(n) <= (3/4)^n sqrt(3/(n + 1)) (PROOFS.md section 3: Stirling's formula with Robbins's bounds, and Jensen's inequality for J ~ Binomial(n, 1/3)), so p(n) = Theta((3/4)^n / sqrt(n)) and T(n) = Theta((4/3)^n sqrt(n)). The restart budget T(n) is 196, 1682 and 22371 tries for n = 6, 12, 20. The implementation computes T(n) in floating point: p(n) T(n) >= ln(10^6) was checked exactly for n = 0..373, and for every n >= 374 it raises OverflowError on every formula without an empty clause, instead of answering (T(374) is about 1.7 x 10^49 tries); formulas with an empty clause are answered False before T(n) is computed. The computed T(n) equals ceil(ln(10^6) / p(n)) for n <= 88 and exceeds it by a relative 10^-12 at most for n <= 373. The O((4/3)^n poly(n)) bound is a worst-case bound. On random and planted satisfiable formulas the walk usually succeeds much sooner. Brute force's O(2^n m) is likewise a worst case: on the unsatisfiable timing family it makes only 6.6 to 8.2 clause checks per assignment (measured for n = 4..14).
notes: Proofs of the claims: PROOFS.md. Related: notes/boundary-2sat-vs-3sat.md (the 2-SAT / 3-SAT boundary) and staging/boolean-satisfiability (later algorithms); the facts they rest on are listed under background.

background.statement: 3-SAT is NP-complete, so a polynomial-time algorithm would imply P = NP. This is the reason for the primary tag T6.
For k-SAT the same random walk runs within a polynomial factor of (2(k-1)/k)^n; k = 3 gives the (4/3)^n base of this entry.
Faster exponential algorithms for 3-SAT are known (PPSZ and its successors); staging/boolean-satisfiability catalogues them with their sources.
2-SAT (at most two literals per clause) is solvable in linear time.
